claims.text: The magnitude and spatial variability of local shear-fault energy govern strength in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Local shear-fault-energy variability governs deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Hard local atomic motifs associated with fault-energy fluctuations impede dislocation motion.
Local fault-energy fluctuations promote non-conventional plastic mechanisms such as deformation twinning.
Fe80−xMnxCo10Cr10 and CrMnFeCoNi are representative metastable FCC multi-component alloys relevant to the proposed mechanism.
Chemical inhomogeneity in metastable complex concentrated alloys produces local variations in planar fault energies.
Controlled thermal treatment or aging can enhance clustering or short-range chemical order while preserving alloy composition.
Enhanced short-range order produces larger spatial fluctuations in local shear-fault energy than a more random solid solution.
Ambient-to-cryogenic temperature changes can alter the deformation modes of these metastable alloys.
At ambient-to-cryogenic temperatures, thermal activation will not override the effects of local fault-energy fluctuations.
Quasi-static deformation isolates the effects of dislocation pinning and twinning.
Spatial fault-energy variations cause dislocations to adopt wavy configurations.
Spatial fault-energy variations cause kinked dislocation configurations and increase the energy barriers for slip.
Regions with higher local fault energy pin or deflect dislocations.
Dislocation pinning or deflection by high-fault-energy regions activates deformation twinning as an alternative strain-accommodation mechanism.
The enhanced-SRO sample will have higher yield strength than the more random baseline.
The enhanced-SRO sample will shift from ordinary dislocation glide toward twinning or other non-conventional deformation modes.

The proposed relationship is limited mainly to chemically complex, metastable FCC alloys with low stacking-fault energy and may cease to dominate when extreme temperatures or strain rates trigger additional transformations or athermal mechanisms.
